text: Linux software doesn't come as a downloaded installer you double-click and click through. Every distro ships a package manager instead, and this lesson covers the two command sets you'll actually use across real cloud servers: apt for Debian and Ubuntu, and yum or dnf for RHEL, Fedora, CentOS, and Amazon Linux.

On Debian and Ubuntu, apt update refreshes the local list of what's available without installing anything, apt upgrade then installs newer versions of packages you already have, apt install adds something new, apt remove takes it away, and apt search looks one up by name. apt-get is the older, more script-friendly version of the same tool.

On RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream, and recent Amazon Linux, dnf — Dandified YUM — is the modern equivalent, with yum as the older tool it replaced and nearly identical syntax between them. dnf check-update lists available updates, dnf update installs them, dnf install adds new software, and dnf search looks one up. The command shapes deliberately mirror apt's, even though the two families are unrelated under the hood.

Line up the two side by side and the pattern repeats across every single task: refresh the package list, install upgrades, install something new, remove it, search for it. Only the command name changes — apt versus dnf — the actual job you're doing, and the order you'd reasonably do it in, stays identical either way.

A real cloud career puts you in front of both families, often in the same week — an Amazon Linux EC2 instance here, an Ubuntu VM there, a legacy RHEL box somewhere else. Knowing both command sets up front means you're never actually starting from zero on an unfamiliar distro you've just SSH'd into. Next up: Chapter 4, and what's actually running on a Linux box right now — processes, services, and systemd.
